articles.title: Channi vs Warring: Why Sachin Pilot may be Congress's best bet in Punjab
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: The Congress leadership last week finally responded to 'Mayday' calls from Punjab rebels and brought in Sachin Pilot, replacing Bhupesh Bag.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Congress leadership last week finally responded to 'Mayday' calls from Punjab rebels and brought in Sachin Pilot, replacing Bhupesh Baghel, to prevent a crash landing of the deeply fractured state unit ahead of the assembly elections early next year.Months of open infighting between Charanjit Singh Channi, the former chief minister leading the rebel camp, and Raja Warring, the state unit chief, not just embarrassed the Congress but also threatened to derail its 2027 campaign.Before being put in the driver's seat in Punjab, Pilot was in charge of Chhattisgarh, where Baghel remains a key Congress leader and former chief minister.Why Congress was forced to budgeThe Congress had sent former Chhattisgarh chief minister Bhagel to Punjab in February this year to defuse the brewing Channi vs Warring crisis in the state unit. Ironically, as things turned out, Baghel faced resistance and became part of the crisis, with the Channi camp openly accusing him of siding with Warring. More so, since July, after the party’s central leadership decided to ignore Channi’s claim for the top post in the state and announced that it would continue with Warring as state Congress president.With several senior state leaders backing Channi, the fight turned ugly and Baghel became ineffective. Congress meetings in the districts saw open “Go back Baghel” chants from Channi supporters, taking the infighting to the streets and embarrassing the top leadership.So, while the ruling Aam Aadmi Party was already in full election mode with chief minister Bhagwant Mann at the centre of its campaign, the Congress was still struggling to get its senior leadership to sit across the table.Not just the AAP, even the BJP and the Akalis had their house in order and were planning their electoral moves on the ground. With the party's 2027 campaign failing to take off under Baghel, the Congress was forced to budge and turn to Pilot.Why Sachin PilotThe Congress decision to send Pilot to Punjab, while ironic, may still be the best bet for the leadership. Sachin Pilot, during his years in the Congress, has seen enough internal wars to know how quickly a fight over one post can turn into a larger battle over leadership, political space and, of course, eventually the chief minister's chair.Throwback to Rajasthan, where he spent years at the centre of a similar leadership tussle with senior leader Ashok Gehlot. Pilot brings something the Congress needs badly right now: the experience of being at the centre of a difficult internal power struggle.Pilot has led the Rajasthan unit, worked closely with the high command, weathered the bitter internal battle, survived the fallout and then rebuilt his position within the Congress.He was appointed Rajasthan Congress chief in 2014, after the party's abysmal performance in the 2013 assembly election. Over the next four years, he emerged as one of the key faces of the party's rebuilding effort before Congress returned to power in 2018. That victory, however, did not give him the chief minister's chair.Ashok Gehlot became chief minister, while Pilot was made deputy chief minister and continued as PCC president. While both sides got something, the arrangement never really settled the rivalry between Gehlot and Pilot.By 2020, those differences exploded into an open rebellion.Pilot left Jaipur with a group of MLAs and challenged the Gehlot government. Congress responded by removing him as deputy chief minister and state president. The Gehlot camp even accused him of working with the BJP. A truce was eventually worked out, and Pilot stayed with Congress.But he never quite returned to the position he had occupied before and has been on the sidelines ever since. He remained a prominent face in the party and was later given charge of Chhattisgarh, but his role in Rajasthan remained limited.It is interesting how, in Rajasthan, Pilot was the leader asking the Congress high command to listen to a dissatisfied camp. In Punjab, he now has to convince dissatisfied leaders to accept the high command's decisions and work together.That may be why Congress believes he is best suited for the job.Baghel gone. Will Warring be next?But will Pilot’s appointment end the crisis in the Punjab unit?Channi's supporters had demanded Warring be removed as Punjab Congress chief, and the Jalandhar MP be declared Congress’s chief ministerial face for the 2027 assembly polls. The Congress has not accepted either of the two demands. So, while Channi has not made any significant gains, Warring has been left wondering if he will be the next to be axed.Warring was picked up to lead and rebuild the Punjab unit after the Congress was decimated in the 2022 assembly polls. Channi, who was the chief minister then, led the Congress to its worst-ever performance in the state. But as is the Congress’s wont, the party kept dilly-dallying on the issue for nearly 4 years. Finally, when the Congress did take a decision, it ended up opening deep faultlines.For now, both camps have welcomed his appointment. Warring said Pilot's energy and dynamism would "for sure" add to the vigour of the party ahead of the crucial polls, while Gurdaspur MP Sukhjinder Singh Randhawa, a close associate of Channi, said Pilot's experience, leadership and connect with the people would give new strength and momentum to the Congress in Punjab.Punjab Congress working president Raj Kumar Verka hopes that under Pilot’s leadership all state leaders would come together. On Monday, he said he was confident that with a strong organisation, collective effort and the energy of party workers, Congress could return to power in the state.Pilot has the experience of being a part of successful strategising in Himachal Pradesh in the previous assembly polls and has also been a senior observer for the Kerala polls, where Congress returned to power after a decade.If Pilot can manage to bring the rival Punjab camps together and help the Congress put up a strong show in 2027, it will add to his standing within the party at a time when Rajasthan is already looking ahead to the 2028 assembly election.There has long been speculation over a bigger role for Pilot in Rajasthan. articles.title: Renoir paintings worth millions stolen in French museum heist
articles.summary: It is the latest in a string of high-profile art thefts in Europe that has again put the security of museums and galleries in the spotlight.
articles.body:
Two paintings by the impressionist artist Pierre-Auguste Renoir have been stolen from a museum in the south of France.

Two thieves broke into the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer early on Tuesday, seizing four paintings but dropping two of the works in the museum gardens as they escaped, local Mayor Bryan Masson said.

The paintings, each worth €9m (£7.7m; $10.4m), are the latest high-profile pieces to have been stolen in a string of recent heists in Europe which have thrust the security of art in galleries and museums into the spotlight.

One of the most high-profile was in October last year, when a brazen heist at the Louvre Museum in Paris saw France's priceless crown jewels being stolen.

CCTV footage captured the thieves entering the Renoir museum gardens by cutting through a fence before they cut through structures holding the paintings' frames in place, the local mayor said.

The alarm went off at 05:48 (05:48 GMT), and police were at the scene within five minutes, Masson explained, saying the thieves fled the scene upon hearing the security alarms.

He later told reporters that the thieves seemed to be "well-equipped" and "well-informed".

They were "wearing helmets, gloves, and combat gear" and carrying "an electric knife and hacksaw," he added.

Investigators have found two zip-up bags at the scene, which may have belonged to the suspects.

The mayor said that two paintings were "abandoned" in the gardens and have now been recovered.

The two paintings that are still missing are:

Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano (1910)

And the two pieces that were recovered are:

"Attacking the Renoir Museum is attacking a part of the history and heritage of Cagnes-sur-Mer," the mayor told reporters at the museum.

"It's Renoir's, it is priceless, you cannot sell it like that," he said.

The Renoir Museum is home to 12 of the famous painter's artworks.

Opened in 1960, it was Renoir's last home before his death in 1919, and also features many things that once belonged to him, including his easel and wheelchair, as well as photographs and personal letters.

"Beyond Cagnes-sur-Mer, this incident should serve as a warning about the protection of our museums, which now face a new form of organised crime targeting works of art," the local French mayor warned.

Masson called on the French government to provide more financial support to local areas and museums to protect artwork from "increasingly organised and determined criminals".

articles.title: Saudi Arabia vows to respond after Houthis attack cities and energy facilities
articles.summary: The Iran-backed Yemeni group's attacks have injured 73 people and caused fires at oil facilities, Saudi authorities say.
articles.body:
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement has attacked energy facilities and other civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia with dozens of drones and missiles, injuring 73 people, Saudi authorities say.

Tuesday's attacks hit four south-western cities, causing fires at oil facilities and installations that led to a temporary halt in operations, according to Saudi Arabia's military and energy ministry.

The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said that its forces would respond to the "dangerous escalation".

The Houthis said the attacks were retaliation for dozens of recent Saudi strikes on areas of north-western Yemen that they control.

On Monday, they accused Saudi Arabia of bombing a prison in the city of al-Hazm and killing at least 11 people. Twenty inmates are reportedly missing under the rubble.

Houthis reportedly kill six in first deadly attack since start of Iran war

Houthi attacks reportedly kill at least 30 Yemeni government forces

Houthi attacks raise fears of wider Middle East conflict and more global economic damage

The spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen, Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki, said the Houthi drone and missile attacks targeted civilian and economic sites in the cities of Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran, and that women and children were among the injured.

An energy ministry statement cited an official source as saying that injuries were also reported after "several energy sector facilities and installations" were targeted.

The attacks "caused fires at several locations, leading to a temporary halt in some operations," they added.

Maliki described Houthi attacks as a "dangerous escalation that confirms the hostile and irresponsible approach of this terrorist militia" and said the Saudi-led coalition would "take all necessary operational measures to deter" the group.

Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea accused the Saudi military of carrying out more than 120 air strikes on the Yemeni provinces of Marib, al-Bayda, Hudaydah, Taiz and Jawf over the past three days, and of committing "grave crimes".

He said the Houthis had responded to this "brutal aggression" with "dozens of ballistic missiles and drones", which he claimed caused "significant damage".

A Saudi-led coalition of Arab states has backed Yemen's government against the Houthis in the country's devastating civil war for more than a decade.

A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.

The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

There has been heavy fighting on Yemen's south-western coast since Thursday, when the Houthis launched an offensive against Yemeni pro-government forces in a bid to take control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.

The fighting has reportedly left more than 300 people dead and displaced 18,500.

The Red Sea has become crucial for oil shipments from Saudi Arabia during the US and Israel's war with Iran, which has led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy defense attorney Kevin Reddington speaks out after mistrial, seeks pardon
articles.summary: Lindsay Clancy’s attorney spoke out for the first time Tuesday since her state murder trial ended in a mistrial, including calling on President Donald Trump to pardon his client.
articles.body: Lindsay Clancy’s attorney spoke out for the first time Tuesday since her state murder trial ended in a mistrial, including calling on President Donald Trump to pardon his client. “I’d like to say that perhaps Donald Trump, who felt compelled to speak out on this case. Mr. President, I would hope that you would consider this young lady. The type of person she is, what she has been through, and consider a pardon,” Kevin Reddington said Tuesday on “Good Morning America.” The request in the wide-ranging interview about the high-profile case was unusual, considering the president can only pardon federal crimes. On Friday, Trump weighed in on the mistrial and said he had been following the case. Reddington did not immediately respond to NBC News’ requests for comment. The White House referred to Trump’s previous comments about the case. Clancy was charged in the strangulation deaths of her three children — Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months old — at their Massachusetts home in January 2023. She had thrown herself out of her bedroom window in a suicide attempt that left her paralyzed. Throughout the trial, Reddington argued that Clancy was in the throes of postpartum psychosis and acted on auditory hallucinations that compelled her to carry out the killings. Prosecutors, however, said that Clancy was aware of her actions and planned out the killings ahead of time. After 38 hours of deliberations, the jury could not come to a unanimous agreement. The judge officially declared a mistrial after Reddington’s last-minute effort for an emergency stay on the decision. Reddington also noted that he believed the 11-1 jury split favored not guilty by lack of criminal responsibility and that one holdout wanted to convict. He does not know that for sure, though, and said he has not spoken with any of the jurors. He was also asked about some of his comments after court Friday, specifically that he said he “crushed the prosecution in court.” “It’s bravado,” he said. “You know, that’s after the fact, and you know, the emotions run high, and we just finished a six-, seven-week trial.” But he added that he didn’t regret the comment and that he thinks the defense was very strong. Although he was angry after the jury was hung, Reddington said, he defends the right of the juror “to be a holdout for forever,” noting that’s how the American judicial system works. Reddington said he was upset specifically because the juror was not following the law. “That’s not right, and that’s why I was upset,” he said. The commonwealth of Massachusetts now has to decide whether to retry Clancy or offer her a plea deal. Reddington said he hopes to work with District Attorney Timothy Cruz to figure something out. “I hope, however, after sitting through this trial and seeing the evidence that was presented from the government, as well as from the defense, that [Cruz] would revisit that issue and hopefully would be able to work something out that would be acceptable to both sides,” he said Tuesday. During the interview, Reddington also spoke about his client, calling Clancy “intelligent,” “hardworking” and an “incredible person.” “I do feel a very strong bond with Lindsay because of the type of person she is,” he said, noting that he has previously said Clancy is like a daughter to him. Patrick Clancy also speaks out Lawyers for Clancy’s ex-husband and the father of the three slain children also spoke out Tuesday, slamming online sleuths and true-crime creators who pushed theories that Patrick Clancy was actually the one who carried out the murders. In a new statement, his lawyers called it a “campaign of misinformation” that was “publishing what they know to be outright falsehoods that Patrick was somehow involved in the death of his young children and other vile claims.” “This campaign, now fueled by insatiable media coverage, remains at a fever pitch and has resulted in real life threats to his reputation, livelihood, and life,” the Tuesday statement said. “Patrick has no choice but to address this situation — with the clear goal of stopping injurious behavior, creating accountability for lies that are self-serving to the perpetrators, and being able to return his attention to what matters: preserving the memory of Cora, Dawson and Callan Clancy and supporting other women facing perinatal mental health challenges,” the statement continued. The statement added that “every appropriate measure will be pursued to hold them accountable, including legally” and that “law enforcement has been notified.” Reddington on Tuesday noted that the Clancy family was torn apart by his client’s postpartum psychosis and blamed one of the doctors she reached out to for help, who he said overprescribed her with psychiatric medications. “I just am horrified at what women have to deal with postpartum,” Reddington told “GMA.” “Dealing with postpartum depression, dealing with God forbid, postpartum psychosis, and the horrific actions that occur as a result of that,” he continued. “People do not understand or know what they are doing, and it is real, and it is frightening.”

articles.title: Panama City's 1914 grammar school survived more than a century and Hurricane Michael; its empty classrooms are now set to become homes
articles.summary: US News: The former Panama City Grammar School on East Seventh Street is finally set to transform. After years of sitting empty and deteriorating, the 1914 bri.
articles.body: The former Panama City Grammar School on East Seventh Street is finally set to transform. After years of sitting empty and deteriorating, the 1914 brick structure in downtown Panama City has found a developer willing to take on its resurrection, WJHG reported. The historic school will now be redeveloped into a brand-new residential project with apartments and townhomes.Old classroom gets a second lifeThe century-old classroom is ready for a transformation. Developer Zachary Seymour will purchase the property and convert it into apartments and townhomes, and city officials have just cleared the financial hurdles to make it happen. The city will waive approximately $375,000 in accumulated code enforcement fines. The city's Community Redevelopment Agency will also provide a $100,000 grant for the development.Discussions about preserving and restoring the century-old brick school building have been going on for years, especially after Hurricane Michael in 2018. The hurricane didn't just damage the building; it broke something fundamental about the structure itself, leaving roofs compromised, windows shattered and doors buckled. For years after the storm, the rundown school sat there.Now the century-old school is finally getting its second life. Under a newly proposed agreement, the city commissioners have cleared a path for the developer to buy the property and start the renovations that have been long overdue.The developer has been given exactly one year to complete the important structural repairs, such as stabilising the roofs, replacing the windows and doors, and addressing the compromised integrity that a 110-year-old building can't ignore. If he misses this deadline, the $375,000 in forgiven fines returns to the property record. It's a stick alongside the carrot. For the preservation efforts, the CRA will grant $100,000. The CRA funds are expected to be formally approved by the commissioners during their next scheduled board meeting.The local leaders are stressing the importance of saving the historic structures. Preserving and restoring the historic structure is the top priority, especially after so much of the local heritage was lost in 2018.“We have very few historic facilities left in our community, especially after Hurricane Michael. Any chance that we have to save one, let’s take advantage of it. Let’s push in every way that we can. And this is one of those efforts that’s been the city. It’s been private people coming in that care to really take the lead in charge to see this come to reality,” District 4 Commissioner Josh Street told the broadcaster.The city's investment reflects its priority. After the storm, cities often have to decide which damaged historic buildings are worth saving. Panama City chose to save this one. The Grammar School's resurrection won't be quick or simple. The structural repairs alone will test the timeline. But for a building that was already vanishing into Panama City's background, the agreement is something close to a second chance.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Yemen’s reignited war fuels a new wave in child recruitment
articles.summary: Yemeni government and Houthi forces are engaged in a new round of fighting.
articles.body:
Sanaa, Yemen – A month ago, a Houthi recruiter in his 40s , approached 16-year-old Abdulkarim in Sanaa and told him about the possibility of being sent to the front line in Marib, where fighting was raging against pro-government forces.

Abdulkarim was promised a Kalashnikov, and a one-month military training course and 50,000 Yemeni rials ($100) , slightly above the local average.

In a country where more than four in five rural children are multidimensionally deprived, the offer was a tempting one. While Abdulkarim was ready to fight, his father, 39, did not approve and so Abdulkarim stayed in Sanaa.

“My father advised me that survival on active front lines nowadays is minimal, and going there is a sure step to death, injury or captivity. I told the Houthi man of my father’s objection, and he left,” Abdulkarim told Al Jazeera.

As Yemen experiences its most intense fighting in years , a new wave of child recruitment in the country is taking shape.

Ali Hazazi, head of the Human Rights and Civil Society Organizations Department at the Office of the President in Aden, told Al Jazeera that his organisation had documented 62 child recruitment cases in the second quarter of 2026 in Houthi-controlled provinces.

“This reflects a systematic policy of child recruitment. The documented cases are just a fraction, as many go unreported,” he said.

Against the backdrop of major offensives on Houthi positions, pro-government forces have captured many child soldiers, including on the al-Dhale front, he said.

“Those children panicked and collapsed when they fell into the hands of government troops, who reassured them that they would not be hurt,” said Hazazi.

Ahmed, 17, has been on the front lines in Hodeidah – a strategically important Yemeni Red Sea port – since May, fighting with the Houthis. He manages to call his family once a week and recently returned home for a week’s leave.

“Members of the Houthi group were mobilising fighters from our area in April. Ahmed said he was ready to join the war and insisted on going. I did not oppose him,” his father, Ismael, 48, who has 10 children, told Al Jazeera.

“Ahmed is a man, no longer a child. I want him to try his luck in this experience. And his monthly salary of 45,000 Yemeni rials, about $80, would help us cover living expenses.”

Ahmed spent his first month learning how to use an assault rifle, shoot from long range and move through areas with landmines.

“He is a young trained fighter today, but I am still worried about his fate, as fighting on the Hodeidah front intensifies,” said Ismael.

The Houthis launched a major offensive against pro-government lines in western Taiz and southern Hodeidah last week, with more than 100 fighters from both sides killed since Thursday.

For some families, the decision to allow children to join the fighting is shaped by a combination of economic hardship, social pressure and ideology.

Ahmed Nagi, a senior Yemen analyst at the International Crisis Group, said that the circumstances surrounding child recruitment in Yemen differ from those in other conflicts.

“In many cases, children are subjected to ideological indoctrination, recruited without meaningful compensation, and sent to the front lines with little or no military training,” Nagi told Al Jazeera.

“Sending a child to a military camp or the front line can sometimes provide the family with some form of material support or irregular income. This may not be a stable salary or a clearly defined package of benefits, but for families living in extreme poverty, even limited assistance can appear better than having no income at all.”

More than half of Yemen’s population does not have reliable access to enough food, with six million people facing “emergency” levels of deprivation that border on famine, the UN’s humanitarian chief, Tom Fletcher, told the UN Security Council in remarks last month.

Social pressure can create a cycle of mobilisation and revenge, with some Yemeni families seeing fighting as a social obligation.

“When a family member is killed, the conflict can become deeply personal,” Nagi told Al Jazeera. “In some cases, this includes children. One death can lead to further mobilisation, which produces more casualties and, in turn, further recruitment.”

Families who strongly align politically with a particular armed group may not see anything inherently wrong in sending their children to fight for the cause. “Instead, they may view it as an act of loyalty, sacrifice or defence of their community,” he said.

Tawfiq Al-Humaidi, head of SAM Organization for Rights and Liberties, which monitors and documents human rights violations across Yemen, said that although the majority of child recruitment cases are happening in Houthi-controlled areas, the movement is not the only actor in this phenomenon.

“The group seeks to replenish the losses of fighters and prepares for new rounds of fighting, and this makes child recruitment an ideal option,” Al-Humaidi told Al Jazeera.

Young Yemenis are often recruited at 17, an age that social and tribal norms equate with manhood, virility, and psychological and mental maturity, he said, and when children traditionally begin to carry weapons.

SAM reported that 11,310 children were recruited or used across 19 Yemeni governorates between 2014 and 2023, including 6,269 children aged 8 to 11.

International law generally prohibits the recruitment and use of children under 18 in armed conflict. The use of children by the military in any situation under 15 is also banned under international humanitarian law.

In 2014, the Yemeni government signed an action plan with the UN to end and prevent the recruitment of children by the Yemeni Armed Forces. In 2022, the Houthis signed a similar UN action plan .

The Houthis have in the past denied enlisting children to fight. But Al-Humaidi said that children in Yemen still undertake military tasks such as guard duties, transporting ammunition, reconnaissance, laying landmines and direct combat.

“As a result, they are exposed to death, injury, and long-term psychological trauma. This is not the fault of children; the recruiters are the culprits,” he said.

“This creates a compounded set of violations: the recruitment of children, their ideological mobilisation, their deployment without adequate preparation, and the lack of any meaningful support or compensation for their families if they are killed.”

Al-Humaidi said that while action plans, such as those signed by the Houthis and Yemeni government, are important, they will not succeed if they remain mere political pledges that lack implementation mechanisms.

Effective measures are needed to prevent children from registering as fighters and to verify recruits’ ages, he said.

He added that child soldiers need effective demobilisation and rehabilitation, including access to education, and that military commanders need to be held accountable.

“The continuation of the war increases the risk, but this does not absolve any party of its responsibility to keep children away from the front lines,” said Al-Humaidi.

articles.title: Widespread flight delays hit major British airports
articles.summary: Flights departing from two of London’s Heathrow Airport have been grounded following a “technical issue.”
articles.body: LONDON — Flights departing from at least two major British airports have been grounded following a “technical issue,” officials said Tuesday. London’s Heathrow Airport said in a statement Tuesday that it was working with Britain’s National Air Traffic Service to resolve the issue, advising passengers to check with their airlines for more information regarding their flights. “Arriving flights are not currently impacted,” Heathrow said, although it advised passengers to check flight times. London Gatwick Airport also said on X that it had been affected, and further north, Manchester Airport took to social media to warn that the issue “may result in delays.” Edinburgh Airport in Scotland issued a similar warning. After earlier blaming a “technical issue,” the National Air Traffic Service said in an update on X that its engineers had “implemented a fix, and our flight system is starting to recover.” Apologizing to passengers for the disruptions, it said flights were “departing and airspace is open, but recovery will take some time.” Heidi Alexander, Britain’s transport minister, also took to social media to apologize. “I know this will be frustrating for passengers and I’m sorry,” she wrote on X. With 84.5 million passengers last year, Heathrow ranked seventh in the table of the world’s busiest airports, according to data published by Airports Council International. Airline Ryanair said in a statement that 65,000 of its passengers were disrupted and 50 scheduled flights were canceled because of the disruption. Travel from Heathrow was severely disrupted in March last year when a massive fire at an electricity substation caused a predawn power outage at the global transport hub. The closure affected more than 1,300 flights and 200,000 passengers. After investigating 600 items of evidence related to the substation, the National Energy System Operator ruled out suspicious activity in a report saying a preventable moisture fault caused the fire, leaving almost 70,000 homes without power.

articles.title: Grocery store switch could save Americans money while shaking up dinner routines
articles.summary: Imported grocery stores hit $56 billion in 2024 sales as younger shoppers seek new flavors at international supermarkets across the country.
articles.body: If you're at a loss for what to make for dinner, a trip to an international supermarket could be just what you need to spark some culinary inspiration — while potentially saving a little money on your grocery bill. Whether you'll actually save, however, depends on what's in your cart. "Savvy shoppers can compare and see whether or not they're getting good deals," Barbara E. Kahn, a marketing professor at the University of Pennsylvania's Wharton School, told Fox News Digital. COSTCO SHOPPERS CHALLENGE INFLUENCER'S CLAIM THAT 'INSANE' CHICKEN MEAL CAN FEED FAMILY OF FIVE "If the supermarket caters to a specialized segment, they may sell enough to reduce their costs of stocking those specialized items," she said. "On the other hand, it's possible that some of these specialized international markets are stocking premium products that you can't get anywhere else, so there's an exclusivity aspect to it, and some of those prices might be higher." Research shows that savings at international supermarkets tend to be category-specific. International grocery stores, particularly Asian chains, have been growing their revenue in recent years. The Associated Press reported in August 2025 on IBISWorld data showing that international supermarkets and small grocery stores took in $55.8 billion in 2024 and had grown roughly 3% a year since 2019, with revenue forecast to top $64 billion by 2029. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Analysts have attributed rising demand to demographic shifts, such as growth in Asian and Hispanic populations, and consumers — especially younger shoppers — seeking new and different flavors. "Everywhere you go in America, you're going to find immigrants, and those immigrants are still cooking their foods from their countries and cultures." In addition to being a place to shop for a deal, international supermarkets can get the creative juices flowing in the kitchen. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Adding just one or two unfamiliar ingredients to your cooking can make a big difference, Palina Louangketh, director of the Idaho Museum of International Diaspora, told the AP. "Coming here to an international market, you get both a dose of cultural experience but also healthy, fresh exotic ingredients," she said. "It doesn't have to be so scary or unique. If you pair your protein with vegetables and with a starch and add savoriness to it — soy sauce, fish sauce, oyster sauce, hoisin sauce — you're covered." You also don't need to whip up an elaborate meal full of exotic ingredients right from the get-go. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "Look at something you really like and see the iterations of it around the world," Beryl Shereshewsky, a New York-based video producer whose YouTube channel focuses on food and cultures from around the world, told the AP. "That way you add a couple of new ingredients and you're trying something new from something that's familiar." International supermarkets can be confusing and intimidating. They may also be difficult to find. Shereshewsky recommended venturing outside your usual neighborhood to find new shops. "I think you would be surprised by how many international markets exist, even in small towns and cities," she said. "Everywhere you go in America, you’re going to find immigrants, and those immigrants are still cooking their foods from their countries and cultures." articles.title: Heathrow and Gatwick among airports hit by air traffic control problems
articles.summary: Departures from a number of airports have been affected by a technical problem affecting air traffic control provider Nats.
articles.body:
Flights from airports in the UK and Ireland are being heavily disrupted by a technical problem affecting the air traffic control provider Nats.

At least 425 flights in or out of the UK have been cancelled, according to tracking website FlightRadar24. EasyJet and British Airways have cancelled more than 100 each.

Nats said just before 17:00 BST that its flight systems were starting to recover.

With few aircraft able to take off, it is understood landings are being restricted, leading to some flights being prevented from departing from overseas airports.

At Heathrow, departures were initially paused around lunchtime. Traffic then resumed, before facing further disruption in the afternoon. It is understood that very few flights are currently taking off. BBC News understands that no flights were going in or out of the airport at 17:00 BST.

Passengers have been advised to contact their airlines to check the status of their flights.

Gatwick said it was currently being affected by the issue, along with other airports.

East Midlands has also been affected, while Manchester Airport warned that some departing flights could be delayed. Passengers have been advised to contact their airlines to check the status of their flights.

Belfast's two airports have both advised passengers to check flight information. The City of Derry Airport said it had experienced some cancellations and delays.

Nats said on Tuesday afternoon that engineers were on site, and it was "working urgently to resume normal operations as quickly as possible".

The organisation apologised for the delays caused and advised passengers to check the status of their flight with their airline. Nats said it would provide updates on and X.

Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said she was aware of the situation, and realised it would be frustrating for passengers.

According to Nats, the flight processing system processes flight plans and other operational information used by air traffic controllers to manage air traffic.

The system continually updates flight information as aircraft progress through UK airspace, helping controllers maintain a safe and orderly flow of traffic.

British Airways said in a statement on its website that passengers should travel to the airport as normal if they have not been contacted by the airline directly. It added that the situation was "entirely out of our control".

Ryanair said affected passengers would be notified.

Phil White from Bexhill told BBC Your Voice that his flight to Lanzarote boarded on time but has been sitting on the tarmac at Gatwick for hours.

"We've been told the radar is down and we can't take off," Phil said.

"It's comfortable enough but the pilots been on every 20 minutes saying they are waiting for information from air traffic control and when he finds anything out he will let us know."

Edinburgh Airport said in a post on X that the issue might affect its operations, while Dublin and Cork airports in Ireland are also experiencing delays.

articles.title: Cheque-bounce case: Actor Rajpal Yadav seeks exemption from surrender, SC says deposit Rs 5 cr first
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Tuesday directed actor Rajpal Yadav to deposit Rs 5 crore with its Registry by Wednesday as a condition for exempting .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Tuesday directed actor Rajpal Yadav to deposit Rs 5 crore with its Registry by Wednesday as a condition for exempting him from surrendering to serve his sentence in a cheque-bounce case involving film producer-financier Murli Projects Pvt Ltd.A bench headed by the Chief Justice, along with Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana, passed the order after Yadav’s plea was orally mentioned before it, as cited by ANI.The court issued a conditional notice on Yadav’s plea challenging the Delhi High Court’s July 10 judgment upholding his conviction and three-month imprisonment in seven cases under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act.The matter will next be heard on September 15.The Delhi high court had earlier directed Yadav to surrender and serve his sentence by September 10 after dismissing his criminal revision petitions challenging his conviction and sentence.The case stems from seven complaints filed by Murli Projects against Yadav, his wife Radha Rajpal Yadav and their film production company over the dishonour of seven cheques issued in connection with financing for the film Ata Pata Lapata.According to the case records, Murli Projects advanced Rs 5 crore in 2010 for completion of the film. As the film’s release was delayed, the parties subsequently entered into a series of agreements, with the repayment amount revised at different stages.Yadav’s petition states that the original transaction was an investment in the film rather than a loan, and that the cheques were issued as security. Under a third supplementary agreement signed in August 2012, eight post-dated cheques were issued, with the repayment obligation linked to the film’s release.The dispute escalated after Murli Projects approached the Delhi High Court in 2012 over the film and obtained an order restraining the petitioners from creating third-party interests in its rights. Subsequently, seven complaints under Section 138 of the NI Act were filed over the dishonour of seven cheques.The petitioners, however, rely on a subsequent consent agreement dated April 21, 2013, under which the parties agreed to a full and final settlement of Rs 10.40 crore, including Rs 40 lakh already paid through RTGS.Four fresh post-dated cheques were issued to secure the settlement. Yadav’s plea says the agreement required the earlier eight security cheques to be returned, but Murli Projects instead proceeded with the dishonoured-cheque cases.The trial court convicted Yadav and the other accused in April 2018 in all seven complaints. Yadav was initially sentenced to six months’ imprisonment and fined Rs 1.60 crore in each case.The sentence was later reduced. On May 22, 2019, he was sentenced to three months’ simple imprisonment and fined Rs 1.35 crore in each of the seven cases, with the sentences to run concurrently.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Adam Carolla says Los Angeles went from a city no one left to a place residents flee for ‘anywhere’ else
articles.summary: The comedian reflected on how dramatically attitudes toward Los Angeles have changed during an appearance on the "Hanging Out with Sean Hannity" podcast.
articles.body: Comedian Adam Carolla says Los Angeles has undergone a dramatic shift, arguing that the city went from a place where residents rarely left to one where they are now willing to move almost anywhere else. "No one ever left LA," Carolla said on Tuesday's episode of the "Hang Out with Sean Hannity" podcast. "You would only leave LA if somebody's dad's company's headquarters moved for some reason or another, or you moved to Hawaii and you were just retiring." "Now, people leave LA, and you go, 'Where are you going?' And they go, ‘Anywhere,'" he added. BILLIONS IN TAXPAYER INCOME ARE LEAVING TWO ICONIC STATES — AS A NEW ECONOMIC MAP EMERGES Carolla said leaving Los Angeles once seemed so unusual that he struggled to understand why anyone would move elsewhere in the country. "When you're from LA, back in the day, if somebody said, 'We're moving to Tennessee...'" Carolla recalled. "I didn't know where Tennessee was. [I would say], 'What are you doing over there?'" The comedian described the shift as a sign of broader problems in Los Angeles, arguing that some people are now leaving out of necessity. "That's a bad sign," he said. AMERICANS CONTINUE VOTING WITH THEIR FEET AS HIGH-TAX CITIES STRUGGLE TO RECOVER "Because [the reason is] not 'our company is relocating,' or 'I'm retiring, and I'm moving to Hawaii.' It's 'I've just got to get out of here.'" Carolla has repeatedly criticized California's Democratic leadership for similar reasons, including Gov. Gavin Newsom and Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, as he has discussed the state’s homelessness crisis, wildfires and what he views as the state's broader decline. articles.title: Remembering Charlie Kirk: Turning Point USA's Andrew Kolvet reflects on conservative group's challenging year
articles.summary: Turning Point USA spokesman Andrew Kolvet reveals how Erika Kirk's leadership prevented the organization from unraveling after Charlie Kirk's death.
articles.body: One year ago this week, Turning Point USA founder and conservative icon Charlie Kirk was assassinated while speaking at Utah Valley University. As the anniversary approaches, his closest allies are still grappling with the tragedy after losing their friend and leader in the prime of his life. Andrew Kolvet, the spokesman for Turning Point USA and a close friend of Kirk's, called the past year "the most challenging year of my life." "Not only did we live through the tragedy of losing Charlie in such a public, horrific way, but we've had to navigate the months afterwards, and try and pick up the pieces and keep charging forward, because I think there would have been a temptation for anybody to just be mired in grief and go into the fetal position after something like that happened. But we also understood that Charlie meant so much to so many people that we had to push forward and keep going," Kolvet told Fox News Digital. TYLER ROBINSON TO FACE TRIAL IN CHARLIE KIRK ASSASSINATION AS JUDGE KEEPS DEATH PENALTY ON TABLE Kolvet, who first met Kirk in 2017 and began working for him in 2018, said he didn't expect a cottage industry of conspiracy theories to emerge from Kirk's murder, but he said he also didn't expect that stories from all over the country from people whose lives Kirk impacted would continue flooding in nearly a year later. Kolvet recounted the story of an Indiana student and high school Turning Point chapter president who clashed with a mother while handing out bracelets. "And she was like, 'You know, Charlie taught me how to stand up for myself and I won't back down. And I'm here because I was inspired to get involved by Charlie, his life and his death, and I won't back down,'" Kolvet said. He continued, "And to see that kind of grit, like a happy warrior from our students and to see their enthusiasm and their willingness to stay engaged, stay fighting — all of those things have been truly remarkable for me to witness and not just witness from afar, hear anecdotes, but to hear their stories personally, for them to come up to me and tell me about it, come on the show and tell us about it has been really amazing." ERIKA KIRK URGES CONSERVATIVE STUDENTS NOT TO BACK DOWN IN FIRST SCHOOL YEAR SINCE CHARLIE'S ASSASSINATION Kolvet credited Turning Point USA's continued success over the past year to Erika Kirk, Charlie Kirk's widow, who was appointed CEO of the group following his assassination, a succession plan Kolvet said Charlie had previously expressed in the event of his untimely death. "The fact that she stepped into that very difficult role in the time and the way and the manner in which she did was so incredibly important, because if you don't know the inner workings of Turning Point, you don't know the way that it's set up, and you don't know all the individual personalities, I'm of the opinion that had she not stepped in when she did and how she did, that you could have seen the unraveling of Turning Point completely," Kolvet said. "She was the one person that could step into that place and have the respect, the love, and the appreciation from all the different parts of the organization and organizations that could have brought everybody together and realized, hey, we're going to fight together, we're going to be together, we're going to rally around each other and make sure Charlie's mission continues to march forward. And she was uniquely the only one, I believe, that could've done that." ERIKA KIRK REFLECTS ON FIRST YEAR OF GRIEF AFTER CHARLIE KIRK'S ASSASSINATION IN NYT ESSAY He touted an "almost 200% growth" in Club American chapters in high schools with over 3,500 across the country and over 1,500 Turning Point college chapters, adding that when he was alive Charlie Kirk believed 1,000 would be the max. Kolvet also pointed to the spike in church partnerships, going from 4,000 to 12,000. Charlie was a thousand percent right for entrusting her with this monumental task should something happen to him... And she stepped into an unimaginable situation and [did] an incredible job with that," Kolvet added.

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy's lawyer hopes for deal with prosecutors after mistrial
articles.summary: Kevin Reddington also asked Trump to pardon Clancy a pardon, during his appearance on Good Morning America.
articles.body:
The lawyer for the Massachusetts woman accused of murdering her three children says he hopes to reach an agreement with prosecutors, after the case ended in a mistrial on Friday.

Kevin Reddington told ABC's Good Morning America programme he was upset a lone member of the jury would not acquit Lindsay Clancy.

To find Clancy guilty, jurors had to be unanimously convinced beyond a reasonable doubt that she intentionally killed her children - Cora, Dawson and Callan - and was not experiencing a psychotic break.

On ABC, Reddington also appealed to President Donald Trump to pardon Clancy. However, she is facing state charges, so the power of clemency would lie with the governor of Massachusetts.

"I would hope that you [Trump] would consider this young lady, the type of person she is, what she's been through, and consider a pardon," Reddington said.

Reddington also said he hoped the district attorney prosecuting the case "would be able to work something out that would be acceptable to both sides".

The BBC has contacted the district attorney for Plymouth County, Massachusetts.

"I'm willing to listen to Tim," Reddington said about District Attorney Tim Cruz, calling him a "hard-charging prosecutor".

The jury - nine women and three men - was weighing a range of options , from not guilty by reason of insanity to manslaughter and first-degree murder.

The 12-member panel appeared to nearly reach a consensus, except for a single holdout who, Reddington said, "would not apply the law of reasonable doubt" as instructed by the judge.

"That's not right," he said. "And that's why I was upset."

Throughout the trial, prosecutors called dozens of witnesses, including several doctors, seeking to prove Clancy had made a calculated decision to murder her children in the basement of their Massachusetts home in January 2023.

Clancy does not deny killing the three, but says there was no premeditation and she was experiencing psychosis at the time. For her to be convicted of first-degree murder, a jury would have to believe she planned the killings.

articles.title: UK bans goods from Israeli West Bank settlements: What that really means
articles.summary: Foreign Minister Ed Miliband said the ban represents a ‘comprehensive reset’ of UK’s policy on Israel.
articles.body:
The United Kingdom has announced a ban on the import of all goods produced by illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, in the country’s most significant policy since London’s historic recognition of Palestinian statehood last year.

In a speech to Parliament, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband accused Israel of carrying out “ethnic cleansing” in Palestine and affirmed that it is official UK policy that the Israeli settlements rapidly expanding across the occupied West Bank are “unlawful”.

He said he did not believe “the British people want us supporting the occupation by accepting products from settlements in our shops”.

Miliband also announced tougher new restrictions on arms sales to Israel.

Israel announced four “counter measures”, including banning 12 British MPs from entering Israel, following his speech.

The UK’s trade ban on goods from illegal settlements comes amid an intensifying wave of Israeli settler pogroms on Palestinian communities in the occupied West Bank and controversial settlement expansions that have prompted a UK-led debate on Europe-wide trade restrictions.

After Miliband’s speech, 12 countries shared a joint statement supporting the two-state solution and announcing their own intentions to impose restrictions on trade with illegal Israeli settlements.

France, the UK, Canada, Denmark, Spain, Finland, Ireland, Iceland, Norway, Poland, Portugal and Sweden called on the Israeli government to immediately halt the expansion of settlements.

Ahead of Tuesday’s announcement, Miliband said new trading bans and sanctions would represent a “comprehensive reset” of the UK’s policy on Israel, amounting to an approach that “not only calls out the injustice [in Palestine], but acts”.

However, he added: “The sanctions regime will target illegal settlements and settlement expansion, not Israel.”

“I can also announce that we’re extending the existing global human rights regime such that it will enable swifter action to deter settlement expansion, including crucially seeking to prevent the development of E1 ,” he added, referring to a proposed settlement in the West Bank which, he said, would divide the Palestinian territory in two and put an end to hopes for a two-state solution.

In support of Israel, Miliband also announced new sanctions against the financing arm of the Lebanese group Hezbollah – Al-Qard al-Hasan – and said the UK will reimpose sanctions on Iran, in line with those imposed by the European Union and United States.

However, he said the UK government “agrees” that settler violence in areas of the West Bank amounts to ethnic cleansing and labelled those carrying it out as “settler terrorists”. He accused the Israeli government of turning a blind eye to the violence and intimidation of Palestinians.

Miliband reaffirmed the UK’s commitment to a two-state solution for Palestine and sharply criticised the rhetoric of Israeli politicians, such as Minister of Finance Bezalel Smotrich, who have called for an end to any notion of a Palestinian state.

Miliband, who is himself Jewish, said the UK government will take a tougher approach towards rising anti-Semitism in the UK. He emphasised that measures by the UK government are being taken against the government of Israel, not the Israeli people, and that targeting Jewish people in the UK for the acts of the Israeli government is “anti-Semitism, pure and simple”.

Britain is a country “that upholds its values at home and around the world, a Britain that fights against oppression and suffering wherever it occurs, a Britain that stands up for what is right”, he said.

The UK ban on trading with illegal Israeli settlements covers the following:

A ban on the import of all goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank.

Sanctions on all organisations, businesses and individuals providing construction, infrastructure, financing or real estate for settlement expansion.

A total ban on advertising in the UK for the sale of properties in illegal settlements in the West Bank.

Sanctions against extremist settlers who have supported or incited violence against Palestinians.

All new export licences for weapons and other exports which “materially contribute to the occupation” will be refused. The UK has already suspended more than 30 arms licences used by the Israeli army in Gaza, he added. The ban on such exports will remain in place as long as the occupation persists, he says.

Products and services from Israel itself.

How much does the UK trade with settlements?

The UK is an important trading partner for Israel as a whole.

Trade between the UK and Israel totalled 6 billion pounds ($8.1bn) in 2025, according to the House of Commons. However, it is difficult to estimate exactly how much of this is from goods produced by settlements, but an estimated 38 million pounds ($51.4m) worth of goods was imported from the occupied territory in 2025, parliament records show.

Precious stones and metals, technical and medical equipment, plastics, machinery and fresh produce including fruit are the major goods imported from Israel. In return, the UK exports, among other things, defence equipment including drones, helicopters and aircraft components.

Between 2024 and 2025, the UK suspended about 30 arms export licences due to Israel’s actions in Gaza. However, exemptions were made for F-35 combat aircraft components, which Israel can access via other partners like the US.

The UK has long tried to distinguish between goods imported from Israel and those from settlements and does not allow such products to access preferential tariffs under a free trade agreement.

To claim preferential tariffs, importers are required to provide UK customs with documentation showing where their goods are manufactured in Israel, and to demonstrate they were not produced in a “location within the territories brought under Israeli administration since June 1967”.

Guidelines were also introduced outlining how products originating from Israeli settlements should be labelled before entering the UK, although concerns have been raised about goods produced in occupied Palestinian territory being mislabelled as “produced in Israel”.

Last May, the UK suspended any negotiations to modernise the trade agreement to cover digital trade and other areas.

Does this mean the UK is removing support for Israel?

No. In his speech to Parliament, Miliband took pains to emphasise that these measures are not being taken against the Israeli people, with whom the British people have “unshakable bonds”.

“Our argument” is not with the people of Israel, but with the “conduct of its government”, he said. “I wholeheartedly oppose the boycott divestment sanctions, or BDS, campaign,” he added.

He said the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel on October 7, 2023 demonstrated the grave threats that Israel faces, and announced that the UK is also implementing new sanctions against the Iran-backed Hezbollah in Lebanon, as well as reimposing sanctions on Iran in line with those of the EU and the US.

To “those who question Israel’s right to exist”, he said: “You are wrong, and we will call you out.”

He added that Hamas must decommission its weapons and dismantle its “terrorist infrastructure” in Gaza. “Hamas can play no role in the future governance of Gaza.”

The foreign secretary said Israel has the right to live without fear.

Miliband said he is “proud” of his own Jewishness and added that his support for the state of Israel is not a “contradiction” of his support for Palestine.

Israel’s Foreign Minister Gideon Saar has announced counter measures against the UK.

It is closing the British Consulate in Jerusalem.

British representatives will be removed from the International Gaza Support Center in Kiryat Gat in southern Israel.

British training of Palestinian Authority forces in the West Bank will be terminated.

Twelve British MPs are banned from entering Israel.

Saar accused the UK government of trying to interfere in Israel’s October election by making this announcement so close to it.

He added that the Israeli public is overwhelmingly opposed to the establishment of a Palestinian state “in the heart of our land”.

On Tuesday, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir called on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to recognise Argentina’s sovereignty over the Falklands, an overseas UK territory that Argentina claims, in retaliation.

Smotrich, Israel’s finance minister, called for the expulsion of the British ambassador.

Burnham spoke with President Donald Trump in a phone call on Monday and stressed the importance of a two-state solution, UK media reported. Trump has, however, not commented on the new ban.

Mike Huckabee, the US ambassador to Israel, has not minced words, however. Over the weekend, he accused the UK government of “Jew hate”. He described any plan for sanctions or trading bans as “discrimination against the Jewish people”.

“I don’t know if [the British government is] really aware of the implications and how it’s going to affect Brits,” he told the UK’s BBC Radio 4 Today programme on Tuesday.

Huckabee claimed that 25 percent of pharmaceuticals in the UK are produced in Israel and that British businesses in the US could face “great damage” in the case of a US reprisal.

Ahead of Miliband’s announcement, Florida Republican Congressman Randy Fine warned that UK companies could be barred from Florida and accused the UK of carrying out a “vanity project in support of Muslim terror”.

On Tuesday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said: “We think it has implications on our ability to make progress with regards to Gaza, on the 20-point plan and the Board of Peace that we’re very committed to. Obviously we’re not going to do what the UK did.”

Palestine’s ambassador to the UK Husam Zomlot said the UK’s decision to impose sanctions and a trading ban was “long overdue” but represented a “turning point in UK-Palestine relations”.

“Today, Britain begins to move from condemnation to consequences, from words to action,” he wrote on X.

Human rights groups have also welcomed the move.

Human Rights Watch said the import ban and sanctions were a “long-awaited and positive change in Britain’s policy”.

Amnesty International UK said the new measures could be “the sea change that is needed”.

However, following Miliband’s address in parliament, the Jewish Leadership Council, which represents Jewish organisations in Britain, accused the government of placing an “increased target on British Jews”.

The council said the move was “deeply irresponsible” and claimed that the government was “yielding to pressure from the most extreme elements of British society”.

The UK’s Chief Rabbi Ephraim Mirvis said it was a “truly a dark day for British Jews” and warned that they would be at greater risk of extremist attacks as a result.

“Today our government has chosen to ignore the deep concerns expressed by so many of us,” he wrote on X. “These measures will succeed only in bolstering the very extremism they seek to target.”

Under former prime minister Keir Starmer, the UK’s Labour Party was strongly criticised for failing to take action over Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza and the pogroms against Palestinian communities in the occupied West Bank. This was an issue that the new prime minister, Andy Burnham, pledged to correct when he took over as leader.

But the ban on Israeli settlement products represents less than 1 percent of UK-Israel trade.

Zena Agha, interim director of the British Palestinian Committee, which advocates for Palestinian rights in the UK, told Al Jazeera the move is a “bare minimum”.

“These are measures we would expect any government to take in accordance with the international legal framework to which it subscribes. So it shouldn’t be celebrated in that regard. Nevertheless, it is something which the previous administration didn’t do, and so it should be welcomed.”

Advocates say the ban’s proper implementation is crucial.

Chris Doyle of the Council for Arab-British Understanding, which has long lobbied for a trade ban with Israel, said it is important to ensure products from settlements are not misleadingly labelled as being from Israel. He also called for a ban on all investments and financial services in the settlements.

“Trading with these settlements should never have been allowed in the first place, built as they are in occupied territory, on the land and resources of Palestinians,” Doyle said.

“I think what we are seeing here is, for the first time, Britain is taking significant action against illegal settlements. It’s long overdue. We’ve heard previous prime ministers from Thatcher to Blair to Cameron all saying settlements are illegal and an obstacle to peace, but they did nothing … It should act as encouragement for other European actors to do the same … Collectively this will make a difference as the EU is Israel’s largest trading partner.”

Given the extent of what he said were Israeli war crimes in Palestine, however, “the UK must be prepared to go further in the event that Israel does not end its settlement enterprise”, Doyle added.

articles.title: 'River Deben at Ufford flowing better than it has for 25 years'
articles.summary: The River Deben is flowing once more after major restoration works are carried out.
articles.body:
A river is flowing better than it has for a quarter of a century after a major restoration but the next stage of works will be "really critical", according to a parish councillor.

Water levels in the River Deben in Suffolk dropped by more than a metre after heavy rain caused a weir structure at Ufford, near Woodbridge, to fall away and a bridge to partially collapse.

While they are still to be fixed, water in the river is again running freely after a multi-agency and community effort saw vital excavations and tree removal take place.

Councillor David Finley, river warden at Ufford Parish Council, said it was a "really exciting moment to actually see the water flowing" again.

"This section of the river used to be cleaned out every five to 10 years, so it's not been like this for 25 years," he said.

"Now, you can see gravel bits and silt bits, and so it's actually creating a really potentially dynamic river."

The collapse in April caused a water-filled crater known as Ufford Hole to drain on to surrounding land, including on a side channel towards the East Suffolk railway line.

It happened after tree roots grew into the weir, which subsequently "fell to pieces", Finley said, resulting in "all the water" rushing towards the Hawkeswade/Lower Ufford Bridge which "cracked" it.

The Essex & Suffolk Rivers Trust said it caused "significant damage to habitats along a large stretch of the river".

A wooden walkway next to the bridge, which allows people to follow a footpath on the river bank, had to be closed off and it is still awaiting repair.

Trevor Gill, from the Lower Deben Riparian Owners Group, said the collapse had a detrimental effect on biodiversity.

"It had a really big impact on nature, but also on people who love this, people who've been fishing and swimming here for decades," he said.

"People were worried about fish dying, which did happen, and it was pretty barren.

"What we've done so far shows people that we are here to get behind this problem and fix it."

After the incident, councils and a consortium of landowners and farmers worked with the Environment Agency and others to form an action plan.

The first phase of that focused on clearing the dried-out channel from Old Melton Mill to Ufford Hole to allow water to flow back to the mill.

Now that has been achieved, attention has turned to repairing the weir before the "winter flood" and also the footpath to restore access.

"The really critical bit is getting this weir sorted out so the water doesn't just accelerate the channel and create real problems further down the river," Finley said.

articles.title: In West Bank, date farmers weigh impact of UK sanctions on Israeli settlers
articles.summary: Palestinians strongly back a ban on settlement goods, but Israel's government says it is a "big mistake".
articles.body:
Juicy brown and ripening yellow dates dangle down from the branches of each palm tree at Israeli settler farms in the Jordan Valley, in the occupied West Bank.

This year, as Israeli growers get ready for a good harvest, they are also preparing for the impact of new Western sanctions against settlements, which are illegal under international law.

The UK government has announced an import ban on settlement goods and said it planned to take action against companies and individuals who provide services for settlement expansion, as part of what it calls a "comprehensive reset" of policy towards Israel following similar moves by several other European countries.

Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain and Sweden have also confirmed their intention to introduce national restrictions, or support European restrictions, on trade in goods with settlements.

Palestinians strongly back such a move, but Israel's foreign minister called it "hostile" and announced a series of counter measures, including the closure of the British consulate in East Jerusalem.

Israeli date farmer Avigdor Arbel, from the settlement of Mesua, calls such boycotts "really disgusting".

Arbel sells his produce mostly to Europe but also to the US and now, India. However, he says the sector is ready for any new UK ban on settler goods.

"As soon as we have a situation of pressure and boycotts, we always break out and look for other markets," he tells me. "So, I believe that if we get to a situation in which there's no place to sell my fruits in Europe, we'll find other markets."

West Bank settlements have expanded rapidly under the current Israeli government, whose ministers say they want "to bury the idea" of an independent Palestinian state - part of the long-standing international formula for peace in the region known as the two-state solution.

At the same time, settler violence against Palestinians has surged to what the UN says is "an all-time high".

With new settler outposts - which are also illegal under Israeli law - now dotting the barren hilltops of the Jordan Valley, there have been repeated attacks on local Palestinians, particularly Bedouin and herding communities.

In January, the last of some 600 villagers fled their homes in Ras Ein al-Ouja after intense harassment by hardline settlers, often backed by Israeli security forces. It was the largest single displacement of a Palestinian community in the past three years.

Further north, in March, Israeli settlers brutally beat and sexually assaulted a Palestinian shepherd during a night raid on Khirbet Humsa.

British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told Parliament on Tuesday that a set of facts on the ground had been created "to make the two-state solution unviable," while "settler terrorism is rampant".

Quoting a former Israeli minister of health and retired brigadier general, Ephraim Sneh, he said the UK government "agrees that there is ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank perpetrated by settler terrorists", to which the Israeli government had "turned a blind eye" or actually supported.

In a significant change of UK policy, he said the government now agreed with the 2024 International Court of Justice advisory opinion that Israel's continued occupation "is unlawful".

As a consequence, Miliband said this should be reflected "in the economic relationships we choose to have with the occupied territories".

"I do not believe that the British people want us supporting the occupation by accepting products from settlements in our shops and supermarkets."

Medjool dates are the main export crop from both Israeli settler farms and Palestinian farms in the Jordan Valley.

"These are rubbish," says Palestinian farmer Abdul Halim Abu Omar, dramatically reaching up and throwing away a handful of shrivelled, yellow dates from a tree in the grove where he works in al-Ouja, north of Jericho.

Around half of the date palms here have no fruit at all. "It's because we lack water," Abu Omar says. His is an extreme case: this year, the trees he cares for have received less than a third of the water they need to thrive.

Access to water has long been a pressing issue in the West Bank.

Interim peace agreements from the 1990s have left a water disparity between Israelis and Palestinians, and Israeli authorities typically prioritise water for settlers over Palestinians' needs.

Recently, in rural areas of the Jordan Valley, almost all of which is under Israeli security and civilian control, extremist settlers have also taken over several freshwater springs.

The Israeli Civil Administration told the BBC that it keeps "continuous contact" with the Palestinian Water Authority and assists in carrying out repairs to water infrastructure.

This harvest time, Abu Omar has few dates that are fit to show local Palestinian exporter Momen Sinokrot. His firm, Palestine Gardens, works with 55 date growers in the Jordan Valley to sell to several European countries, including the UK.

Sinokrot believes that if more states ban settlement trade this could curb settlement growth.

"Settlers are very active in the Jordan Valley... and they are not obeying any laws or rules or anything even from the Israeli army itself," he says.

"They are going to the fields of the growers, they are stealing from them, and they are controlling more and more land."

Israeli-state support for settlements, as well as their relatively easy access to global markets, means that Palestinian farmers struggle to compete. Palestinian businesses face greater restrictions and costs to export across Israeli-controlled borders.

Palestinians want the wide swathe of fertile land in the Jordan Valley - along the West Bank's border with Jordan - as part of their own hoped-for future state, along with the rest of the West Bank and Gaza, with East Jerusalem as its capital.

However, Avigdor Arbel, the settler date farmer, does not believe that his country will ever give up the Jordan Valley. He has lived there since the 1970s.

Within years of Israel's capture of the West Bank from Jordan in the 1967 Middle East War, the Israeli government began encouraging its citizens to move to this area to counter what it saw as the security risk along the border.

More than 500,000 Israelis live in settlements in the West Bank, not including Israeli-annexed East Jerusalem, alongside three million Palestinians.

There are 340 settler outposts in the Palestinian territory along with 146 settlements, formally recognised by the Israeli government, according to the Israeli anti-settlement group Peace Now.

Current UK and EU laws require labels for settlement goods. Agricultural produce commonly exported includes mangoes, avocados, herbs and grapes.

There have been questions raised about how a ban on settlement goods would be enforced.

A recent report by the legal advocacy group Global Echo found that some settlement fruits and vegetables sold in Europe were inaccurately identified as coming from Israel - or mingled with produce from inside Israel's internationally-recognised borders.

However, the report's author, Jessica Stober, suggests that a UK ban on settler goods would greatly increase the financial costs associated with any such fraudulent practices. Instead of a seller being fined for misrepresenting their goods, the shipment would be returned.

"A ban is more self-enforcing because you have involved the private sector and it becomes commercially unviable for them to deal in settlement goods," Stober says.

"I would also say that a whole new set of measures become available to the UK government under a sanctions regime, under a ban, including civil and criminal penalties that make compliance much more likely."

Israel's Foreign Minister, Gideon Saar, responded quickly to the UK's announcement, branding the move "morally distorted" and constituting a "blatant interference in the affairs of a sovereign state and in its electoral process", referring to Israel's general election in late October.

He announced "a series of Israeli countermeasures", including the closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem and the removal of British representatives from the US-led International Gaza Support Center (IGSC) in Kiryat Gat, which is in charge of co-ordinating the shaky ceasefire in the Gaza Strip.

"The message to every government that harms us is clear: whoever acts against Israel, Israel will act against them, and they will lose their influence and relevance in the region," Saar warned.

Last month, Israel expelled two Dutch diplomats from the IGSC, after the Netherlands banned trade from settlements.

Other European countries that have already imposed a ban on settlement goods or trade restrictions - arguing it is a legal obligation - include Ireland, Spain and Belgium.

Now, the new action by the UK looks set to put a new, heavy strain on its relations with Israel.

articles.title: Sudan's healthcare system on brink of collapse after cuts, medical charity MSF warns
articles.summary: Médecins Sans Frontières is urging world leaders to increase funding to help the millions who need aid.
articles.body:
Sudan's fragile health system is on the brink of collapse as global funding cuts have led to the closure of healthcare facilities across the country, Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) has warned.

Dozens of organisations were unable to find alternative funding after the US - the largest donor to Sudan - closed USAID, its body for delivering foreign aid, last year, the medical charity said.

MSF urged world leaders gathering at the UN General Assembly in New York to take action.

The war that erupted in April 2023 between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) has created one of the worst humanitarian crises in the world, with more than 33 million people needing medical assistance.

MSF said while the US was still the largest donor to Sudan, existing grants to many USAID-funded organisations ran out in June - as European governments were also reducing international assistance.

According to the Paris-based Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), international aid fell globally by 21.3% in 2025 compared to the previous year.

A simple guide to what is happening in Sudan

Sudan's invisible children - born in war with no legal identity

"War is driving Sudan's needs; funding cuts are shrinking the response," said Muhammad Ibrahim, the head of charity in Sudan.

"MSF's work in Sudan is privately funded. But when funding disappears from other health services, clinics close, patients have fewer places to go, and pressure shifts to the facilities that remain, including ours."

This has meant that patients often have to make dangerous and long trips to get treatment.

"After a longer and more expensive journey, patients often arrive in a much more serious condition, and the hospital may already be full," explained Sebastián Traficante, MSF's emergency co-ordinator in the western region of Darfur, which has experienced much of the fighting over the last three years.

Between January and April 2026, MSF saw admissions jump by 22.5% in facilities it supports in central Darfur, when compared to the same time last year.

In May alone, 45 healthcare centres in the area had stopped receiving funding, it said.

According to MSF, the closure of frontline services was putting other hospitals under severe strain - as they were losing their capacity to function and medicines were disappearing.

It gave Gedaref state's Tanedba camp, where 18,400 people who have fled their homes live, as an example. Its maternity and surgical wards have closed down after a humanitarian organisation left in June.

As a result, MSF is now running an emergency room there, but pregnant women who need surgery to deliver a baby, have to travel three hours to the nearest city.

In the Um Rakuba camp - also in Gedaref - the number of aid agencies working there has dropped from 35 in 2021, to less than 10.

According to the charity, the camp currently hosts around 17,000 people, most of whom are women and children.

"If support does not increase, more patients will face longer journeys, fewer treatment options and greater risk of arriving too late for care," MSF's UK humanitarian representative Liz Harding said.

At the same time as the health system was struggling with funding, attacks on healthcare workers were continuing, MSF said.

In 2025, Sudan saw 1,620 people killed in attacks on medical facilities - which the charity said accounted for 82% of all global deaths from attacks on healthcare worldwide.

According to the UN, more than 19.5 million people are also experiencing "crisis levels" of food insecurity and more than five million are facing "emergency levels of hunger".

The fighting shows no sign of easing - despite the expected arrival of international diplomats in the Sudanese capital, Khartoum, for consultations aimed at ending the civil war.

Reports from North Kordofan state on Tuesday say at least 11 people have been killed in a drone attack on the army-controlled town of Umm Ruwaba. According to medical sources, the projectile struck a crowded courtyard in a court complex.
