articles.title: In 2023, an Australian cattle station sold for $40 million with plans for a major carbon project; three years later it has resold for $26 million after the project never happened
articles.summary: Real Estate News: A huge cattle station in Australia’s Northern Territory, bought for A$40 million during the height of the carbon farming boom, has been resold for A$2.
articles.body: A huge cattle station in Australia’s Northern Territory, bought for A$40 million during the height of the carbon farming boom, has been resold for A$26 million after plans for a major environmental project fell apart. Benmara Station, a 451,176-hectare pastoral property on the Barkly Tableland near the Queensland border, has changed hands after its value fell sharply. According to ABC News, the 35 per cent drop in price shows how Australia’s northern pastoral property market is adjusting after corporate buyers once paid high prices for land with carbon offset potential. The property was bought in May 2023 by Sydney-based agricultural investment firm Wealthcheck, managed by Sam Mitchell, in partnership with global energy trader Hartree Partners. Real estate company LAWD negotiated the off-market deal, which involved the sale of the property without livestock. At the time, the high price was linked partly to expectations that the property could generate carbon credits alongside cattle production.A speculative boom meets regulatory delayWhen Wealthcheck and Hartree Partners bought Benmara Station in 2023, Australia’s carbon market was gaining strong momentum through Human Induced Regeneration (HIR) projects. The HIR scheme allowed landowners to earn Australian Carbon Credit Units (ACCUs) by allowing native vegetation to recover through lower livestock numbers and changes to land management. Benmara Pastoral Pty Ltd registered the Nicholson River Carbon Project over 452,542 hectares with the Clean Energy Regulator in September 2023. The project aimed to create permanent native forests through assisted natural regeneration. However, the regulatory situation soon changed. The federal government closed the HIR method to new projects and promised a replacement system called the Integrated Farm and Land Management (IFLM) method. But development of the new method faced repeated delays, creating uncertainty for carbon developers and institutional investors.According to research published by Beef Central, Hartree Partners pointed to continued uncertainty over the carbon market transition as a key reason for leaving the investment. Wealthcheck later entered liquidation in 2024, leaving Hartree Partners as the main vendor trying to sell the property. In December 2025, the Nicholson River Carbon Project was officially revoked under section 30 of the CFI Rule. This formally ended the property’s carbon plans before any credits were issued or commercial benefits were gained.Pastoral operations and asset restructuringDespite the collapse of the carbon project, Benmara Station still has strong value as a traditional cattle property. Located about 100 kilometres west of the Northern Territory-Queensland border, the station includes alluvial floodplains, sandstone plains and black soil downs. The land has an estimated carrying capacity of 17,500 adult equivalent cattle. Real estate company CBRE Agribusiness, represented by agents Andrew Loughnan and John Harrison, was appointed to run an Expressions of Interest campaign for the property. Before the sale, the station had been heavily destocked for about 18 months, allowing its pastures to recover after good rainfall across the Barkly region. Speaking to Property Markets News during the sales campaign, CBRE agent Andrew Loughnan described the condition of the property. "Benmara has been largely destocked over the past 18 months," Loughnan said. "During this period, the property has benefited from good rainfall and better pasture growth, making the clean skin cattle an attractive prospect for an astute operator." The vendors also carried out improvements across the property. CBRE agent John Harrison said the station had reliable water infrastructure and an ongoing fencing replacement programme along the eastern boundary and inside its paddocks. Existing facilities include a central homestead compound with two main residences, staff accommodation, machinery sheds and cattle yards.Market correction across the northern pastoral sectorThe A$26 million resale of Benmara Station represents a A$14 million loss compared with its 2023 purchase price. It highlights the sharp correction in property values after carbon speculation helped push prices higher.Before the 2023 deal, the station was owned by pastoralist Malcolm Harris, who bought it in 2016 for A$12 million and invested in water points and internal fencing. The jump to A$40 million in 2023 marked the height of institutional interest in combining northern Australian cattle production with carbon credit opportunities.Analysis from Carbon Pulse and agricultural market reports suggests that pastoral properties across the Northern Territory are now being valued more on traditional factors such as cattle carrying capacity and livestock returns, rather than expected income from carbon projects.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Britain’s dramatic crackdown on Israeli settlements sparks fierce response as US blowback looms
articles.summary: Ed Miliband announced U.K. sanctions targeting Israeli West Bank settlements, prompting U.S. Ambassador Mike Huckabee to warn of economic consequences.
articles.body: The United Kingdom unveiled sweeping new measures targeting Israeli settlements in the West Bank on Tuesday, triggering an immediate diplomatic rupture with Israel and a sharp warning from a senior Trump administration official. Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar announced Tuesday, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s approval, that Israel would close the British Consulate in Jerusalem and impose a series of countermeasures in response to the U.K. sanctions. The Israeli measures also include removing British representatives from the International Gaza Support Center in Kiryat Gat, ending British activities training Palestinian Authority forces in the West Bank and denying entry to 12 British elected officials and other British nationals whom Israel accused of antisemitic or anti-Israel activity. UK MOVES TO SANCTION ISRAELI SETTLEMENTS AS PM BURNHAM RISKS CLASH WITH TRUMP: REPORT "Measures against Israel will not go unanswered," Sa’ar said. "Whoever acts against Israel, Israel will act against them, and they will lose their influence and relevance in the region." The escalation came hours after Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told Parliament that Britain would ban imports of goods from Israeli settlements, target companies and individuals facilitating settlement expansion, and refuse licenses for arms and other exports that materially contribute to the occupation. The move is part of a coordinated push with France, Canada and other European partners amid what the governments described Tuesday as "unprecedented levels of settler violence and settlement expansion" in the West Bank, including Israel’s E1 project, which they argue threatens the viability of a future Palestinian state. The measures come just weeks before world leaders gather for the U.N. General Assembly in New York and less than two months before Israel’s Oct. 27 election, adding diplomatic and political stakes to an already strained relationship between Israel and several of its traditional Western allies. At the same time, the foreign ministers recognized Israel’s "legitimate security interests" and reiterated their condemnation of Hamas’ Oct. 7 terrorist attack, which they described as "the worst antisemitic massacre since the Holocaust." They said their objective remained a two-state solution allowing Israel and "a sovereign, democratic and viable Palestinian state" to live side by side in peace and security. UK DEFENSE SHORTFALLS HIGHLIGHTED AS BRITAIN AVOIDS IRAN OFFENSIVE ROLE AMID TRUMP CRITICISM The timing has also become a political issue inside Britain. An unnamed Labor MP told The Telegraph that Prime Minister Andy Burnham had faced pressure from colleagues worried about Gaza-related campaigning and losing seats to the Greens, while Israeli officials have accused London of trying to influence Israel’s election — claims the British government rejects as it frames the measures as an effort to preserve the two-state solution. "Today, I announce that the official view of the British government is that the occupation is unlawful," Miliband told lawmakers Tuesday. Miliband opened the statement by describing himself as a "proud British Jew" with "the deepest gratitude to the State of Israel," recalling how his grandmother found refuge there after losing her husband and 60 other family members at the hands of the Nazis. He stressed that the measures were aimed at settlements rather than Israel itself. "The sanctions regime will target illegal settlement and settlement expansion. Not Israel," Miliband said, adding that Britain would continue to support trade with Israel inside the Green Line and that he "wholeheartedly" opposed the broader Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement. Miliband also condemned rising antisemitism in Britain, saying, "Holding British Jews responsible for the actions of the Israeli government is antisemitism, plain and simple." He reaffirmed Israel’s right to defend itself against terrorism, called for Hamas to disarm and dismantle its terrorist infrastructure under the U.S. -led 20-point Gaza plan, and announced sanctions against Hezbollah financing institution Al-Qard Al-Hassan. He also said Britain was reimposing major economic sanctions on Iran and would continue security cooperation with Israel against shared threats. The measures drew immediate criticism from U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, who warned in an interview with BBC World Service Newsday that Britain could face economic repercussions in the United States. ISRAELI OFFICIAL SAYS EU SANCTIONS REVEAL ANTISEMITISM HIDING BEHIND 'SOCIALLY ACCEPTABLE MASK' "I think without a doubt there will be," Huckabee said when asked whether the U.K. should expect consequences. Huckabee pointed to Florida and other states with anti-boycott laws, arguing that British companies could face restrictions on doing business there. "If the Brits do something like this with a partner, Israel, then they will not be able to do business in Florida," he said, warning of a "huge economic impact on British businesses." He also challenged Britain’s policy on substantive grounds, arguing that Israel is permitted under the Oslo agreements to build communities in Area C and predicting that the sanctions would have "a very negative effect that does not meet whatever goal maybe that the Brits have." In a separate portion of the BBC interview, Huckabee said, "I feel like that it's a discrimination against the Israeli government. It's a discrimination against the Jewish people. And I don't understand the rationale." The Trump administration also made clear Tuesday that Washington would not join the coordinated sanctions push. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the United States does not want to see "anything destabilizing" in the West Bank, but said Washington would not follow Britain, France and Canada in blocking imports from Israeli settlements, according to Reuters. IS ISRAEL REALLY ISOLATED? POLLS AND DIPLOMACY POINT IN OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS Sa’ar also accused London of interfering in Israel’s election campaign and said the settlement sanctions were driven by domestic British politics ahead of the Labor Party conference. "The British move is morally distorted and constitutes blatant interference in the affairs of a sovereign state and in its electoral process," he said. Israeli President Isaac Herzog called Britain’s move a "grave miscalculation" Tuesday and argued that it amounted to "gross interference" in Israel’s upcoming election, according to a statement from his office. Nitsana Darshan-Leitner, president and founder of the Tel Aviv-based Shurat HaDin-Israel Law Center, also criticized the measures, arguing that the economic impact would be limited while the political consequences could be significant. "These sanctions are not serious economic policy; they are political theater staged at Israel’s expense," Darshan-Leitner told Fox News Digital. She disputed Britain’s legal characterization of the territory, saying, "The territories are disputed, not sovereign Palestinian land, and their future must be negotiated by the parties under the Oslo framework." Darshan-Leitner also argued that because little of the roughly $8 billion in annual U.K.-Israel trade originates in West Bank settlements, the measures would have little direct economic effect while potentially influencing Israel’s political debate ahead of elections. Miliband, however, argued that failing to act would allow continued settlement expansion to destroy the possibility of a two-state solution. He focused particularly on Israel’s E1 project east of Jerusalem, which Britain and numerous other governments say threatens the territorial viability of a future Palestinian state. Sa'ar rejected Britain’s position that the E1 settlement project threatens the viability of a future Palestinian state. UK PINS STRING OF ANTISEMITIC ATTACKS ON IRAN-LINKED GROUP, BANS IRGC The policy has also exposed divisions within Britain. Conservative lawmaker Tom Tugendhat acknowledged in Parliament that illegal settlements were wrong and that some settlers had committed "outrageous abuses" against Palestinians, but argued that the government’s response risked hurting ordinary Israelis and Palestinians. "What we reject here is not the intent, but the performative politics," Tugendhat said, warning against acting without sufficiently broad international support. Miliband rejected arguments that the measures were intended to isolate Israel. articles.title: Lane Kiffin urges LSU fans to show up for Louisiana Tech game, tells them to start drinking at 7AM
articles.summary: Lane Kiffin challenged LSU fans to start drinking at 7 a.m. and pack Death Valley for Saturday's Louisiana Tech game after the Clemson blowout.
articles.body: You can't drink all day if you don't start first thing in the morning. That's not verbatim the message LSU head coach Lane Kiffin is sending his school's fanbase heading into Week 2 of the season, but it's one he's implying. Fresh off a 51-10 thrashing of Clemson to open up the Kiffin tenure in Baton Rouge, the Tigers welcome Louisiana Tech to town on Saturday evening. The atmosphere with the Bulldogs in town will pale in comparison to what was witnessed in Death Valley for the season opener against the Tigers. Kiffin knows that, but it isn't stopping him from challenging the fanbase to show up and show out. LSU HAD A REVIVAL, CLEMSON WAS AT A FUNERAL: LANE KIFFIN’S DEBUT SENDS A LOUD MESSAGE TO COLLEGE FOOTBALL "Don’t let the opponent dictate how you are a fan. We challenge our players to do that, so, the fans, too," Kiffin told reporters on Monday. "If you’ve got to have a mock Saturday or put up a stage of 'College GameDay' — whatever it is. Come out here early; come out here and start drinking at 7:00 a.m.." "Everything’s got to be the same as last Saturday," he continued. "I challenge our fans the same thing. The fans were electric. The whole walk, the beginning of the game, the first quarter – you could feel it coming down on the opponent. People who have been here a long time, they said it was the loudest, intense feelings they felt ever." Kiffin urging fans to come and support his team against a not-so-flashy opponent is nothing new, nor is it a tactic exclusive to him. The 51-year-old coach issued the same sort of statements during his tenure at Ole Miss when the Rebels welcomed smaller, out-of-conference opponents to Oxford. Most other coaches of Power Four programs face the same challenge of having fans show up – which translates to spending their money – at games that aren't exactly circled on the calendar. As for Kiffin's joke about LSU fans pouring a cocktail at 7 a.m. before the Tigers kick off at 6:30 p.m. on Saturday against Louisiana Tech, that's a challenge plenty of fans in Baton Rouge will accept.

articles.title: Hungary expels 10 Russian diplomats, Moscow promises harsh response
articles.summary: Russia promises ‘harsh and painful’ response following Hungary’s expulsion of its diplomats.
articles.body:
Hungary has ordered 10 Russian diplomats to leave the country, accusing them of “unacceptable” activities that it says are incompatible with their diplomatic status.

Anita Orban, Hungary’s deputy prime minister and foreign minister, said on Tuesday that the decision to protect “Hungary’s security and sovereignty” does not mean the country is “breaking off diplomatic relations with Russia”.

Russia promised a “harsh and painful” response, the country’s Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova told Russia’s TASS news agency.

Hungary was one of the few European Union allies to Russia after its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Under the previous government, Budapest’s relations with Moscow were warm.

Former Prime Minister Viktor Orban (not related to current Deputy Prime Minister Anita Orban), who lost the elections last April after 16 years in power, reportedly told Russian President Vladimir Putin: “I am at your service” during last year’s phone call.

Hungary took a “legitimate decision”, EU spokesman Christian Wigand told journalists, adding that the EU “will continue to closely coordinate” the situation.

Many EU member states expelled Russian diplomats following Moscow’s all-out war on Ukraine, but Hungary was not one of them until now.

articles.title: Video captures grocery store manager's daring rescue of toddler who ran into oncoming traffic
articles.summary: Security footage captures Luis Cruz diving into a busy Puebla, Mexico, road to rescue a 3-year-old girl moments before a minivan crosses her path.
articles.body: A supermarket manager in Mexico leapt to action Sunday, diving into the road to save a 3-year-old girl from oncoming traffic, security footage shows. Luis Cruz, a manager at the Super King El Rey del Ahorro grocery store, sprinted after the girl who had wandered into the busy road and grabbed her while diving to the ground moments before she would have been hit by a silver minivan. The girl had run out of the Puebla, Mexico, supermarket around 2 p.m. local time after slipping out of her mother’s grip, according to Mexican news outlet Tribuna Noticias. The girl was initially chased by a woman, but the woman slipped and fell before she could grab the child. WATCH: ICE OFFICER MAKES HEROIC RESCUE AFTER 6-YEAR-OLD GIRL HAS POOL EMERGENCY Video shows Cruz quickly tackling the girl to the ground moments before a minivan crossed the lane she would have entered had Cruz not stopped her. OFF-DUTY ICE OFFICER RELIES ON 'SIXTH SENSE' TO SAVE DROWNING CHILD BEFORE DELIVERING MESSAGE TO CRITICS As car horns honk, Cruz grabs the girl, pulling her backwards as they both tumble safely to the ground in the lane closest to the store while the minivan screeches to a halt in the middle lane. The grocery store, according to Tribuna Noticias, awarded Cruz with 20,000 Mexican pesos – roughly $1,184 – for his heroics. CALIFORNIA LIFEGUARD SPEAKS OUT ON HEARTSTOPPING OCEAN RESCUE: 'I LOVE WHAT I DO' Cruz also reportedly said he didn't think before taking action, and that as a father himself he was driven by paternal action. articles.title: Meet Anvith Yalamanchili, the 17-year-old Dubai student who watched his brother’s school commute triple to 45 minutes and built a free carpool service that drew 1,000 sign-ups
articles.summary: Middle East News: When a student's morning school journey in Dubai Sports City suddenly tripled from 15 minutes to 45 minutes after three new campuses opened nearby, hi.
articles.body: When a student's morning school journey in Dubai Sports City suddenly tripled from 15 minutes to 45 minutes after three new campuses opened nearby, his older brother decided to find a way to solve the traffic problem. Anvith Yalamanchili, a 17-year-old International Baccalaureate student at Dwight Global, created a free, web-based carpooling platform to reduce the number of private cars filling the area's roads. What started as an effort to make his brother's morning journey easier has since grown into a larger organised initiative. According to UAE news outlet The National, the platform, called Community Carpool, has now attracted more than 1,000 registered users across Dubai. "Three new schools opened in the same area, which caused an increase in cars in that area, causing traffic and delays," Yalamanchili told The National. "I noticed a lot of these cars were coming from the same communities, like Arabian Ranches or Sports City, and they all had empty seats. It made me realise people should be able to carpool and that would speed up travel times at the busiest time of day."Algorithmic matching replaces manual mappingAt first, Yalamanchili handled the carpooling arrangements himself. He marked users' locations on digital maps and manually looked for people whose routes could be combined. "In the beginning, I was manually matching people who had signed up on a map," Yalamanchili explained to The National. "I would put pins down and try to see how far everyone was away from each other. But then I realised that the more people involved, the more difficult that was to do, so I created a system." To automate the process, Yalamanchili built a website, communitycarpool.org, using the Haversine mathematical formula. The system calculates the distance between two points on the surface of a sphere. This allows it to match users based on their locations, travel schedules and personal preferences. Unlike commercial ride-hailing services, the platform does not require an app download, subscription fee or extensive data tracking. In an interview with Gulf News, Yalamanchili said the aim was to make carpooling as simple as possible for families and commuters. "The core idea is simplicity. There is no app to download, no logins and no unnecessary data collection," Yalamanchili told Gulf News. "We are fully aligned with GDPR principles, meaning users have complete control over their information. The goal was to remove every possible barrier so that participating feels natural rather than like extra effort."Privacy protection and corporate backingTo address concerns about sharing rides with strangers, the browser-based platform uses an anonymous matching system. The system checks routes and alerts potential matches without revealing personal contact information until both users agree to share it. "There are no fees at any point, so there is no financial barrier. The matching process is anonymous until both sides provide their acceptance, which removes the social awkwardness," Yalamanchili told Gulf News. "And users don't need to actively search through others' routes. The system scans and notifies them when a suitable match is found, which saves time." The platform received a major boost when UAE property developer Damac Properties began using it for its employees. According to Gulf News, Damac executive Nicola Spadoni contacted Yalamanchili after seeing details of his work in a community messaging group. This eventually led to the system being introduced to Damac's 3,500 employees.Expanding the team for broader adoptionYalamanchili has since built a small team of student interns who help promote the free platform in local schools and support its technical maintenance. While established transport companies and technology firms continue to offer paid school transport services in the UAE, Yalamanchili sees his non-commercial platform as a simple, community-led alternative. "I want this to grow as much as possible in the UAE, and to expand in other areas of the world with similar traffic situations," Yalamanchili told The National. "I think places like India and some cities in America could really benefit from this. My parents and friends have signed up, and the feedback has been quite positive."Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Blind Huddersfield man sentenced for 150-mile drive while drunk
articles.summary: Anthony Hall, 50, took his partner's car and drove at night from Huddersfield to near Carlisle.
articles.body:
A blind motorist who took his partner's car and drove for 150 miles (240km) at night while drunk has been handed a suspended sentence.

Anthony Hall, 50, who does not have a driving licence, was stopped by police on the M6 near Carlisle at 01:45 BST on 29 June after he was seen swerving the Vauxhall Meriva between lanes and onto the hard shoulder, a court was told.

Hall told police he had driven from his home in Huddersfield after he and his partner had drunk four bottles of wine.

Kirklees Magistrates' Court heard Hall, of Lees Close, had admitted charges including dangerous driving at a previous hearing and was sentenced on Tuesday to 36 weeks in prison, suspended for 18 months.

Hall had also admitted drink-driving, driving without a licence or insurance and taking a car without consent.

The court heard that in the early hours of 29 June, police received information there was a driver on the M6 northbound who was under the influence and was blind.

Hall was pulled over by a police officer after the Vauxhall was seen swerving near junction 42.

The officer who stopped Hall could smell alcohol on his breath and, when asked about this, the 50-year-old said he and his partner had drunk wine.

Hall told the officer he had gone blind about two years ago but could see some lights and he explained that while on the motorway he had followed an HGV's lights.

The distance Hall had travelled was about 150 miles and he had taken the car from his partner without permission, according to police.

When he was breathalysed at the side of the road, Hall gave a reading of 50 micrograms of alcohol per 100 millilitres of breath.

At a police station later, he gave a reading of 46 micrograms of alcohol per 100 millilitres of breath.

The drink-drive limit in England and Wales is 35 micrograms of alcohol per 100 millilitres of breath.

Hall told police he had planned to drive to Scotland and wanted to escape his home, his relationship and his finances.

The court heard he had stopped for fuel at an unknown location where an attendant had filled up his car.

In mitigation, Adele Graham said her client had no previous convictions and he had suffered a breakdown before setting off on the journey.

Hall had felt trapped in his own home and wanted to get as far away from his life there as possible, she said.

"This was an individual in crisis making a poor decision while in crisis," she said.

Sentencing Hall, magistrate Tracey McErlain-Burns said Hall was of previous good character and had some difficult personal circumstances.

She explained that while the custody threshold had been crossed, she had decided to suspend any custodial sentence.

Hall was sentenced to 36 weeks in prison, suspended for 18 months. Meanwhile, he was told he must carry out rehabilitation activities and abstain from alcohol for 90 days.

Hall was also disqualified from driving for 12 months even though he did not have a licence at the time of the incident, and he was ordered to pay £272 costs.

articles.title: Israeli academia accused of systemic apartheid against Palestinians
articles.summary: A legal report exposes how Israeli universities use a dual-track disciplinary system to target Palestinian students.
articles.body:
One Palestinian student found herself facing permanent expulsion and the revocation of all her academic credits at Zefat Academic College in Israel, after posting a video of a religious preacher praying for the people of Gaza.

Another Palestinian student, at the Technion-Israel Institute of Technology in Haifa, was suspended for posting a Quranic verse.

The individual cases reflect a sweeping institutional crackdown documented in a report this week by Adalah , the Legal Center for Arab Minority Rights in Israel, since Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began in October 2023.

Adalah received more than 130 inquiries from Palestinian students facing disciplinary proceedings across approximately 40 institutions. More than three in four of the targeted students were women.

The report concluded that Israeli academia has established a two-track disciplinary system amounting to apartheid within higher education.

Palestinians go through an “administrative track”, characterised by the suspension of standard procedural protections and the presumption of innocence.

Meanwhile, Jewish Israelis have “constitutional track” protections, grounded in the rule of law.

The report revealed a host of systemic procedural flaws in the monitoring of Palestinian students, notably the reliance on automated software like Google Translate to interpret Arabic texts, prayers, and cultural expressions.

Adi Mansour, an Adalah affiliate attorney, European University Institute PhD researcher and co-author of the report, said this shouldn’t be viewed as a calculated tactic.

“We view it as institutional incompetence, compounded by an unwillingness to both understand the complexity of language and discourse, and to engage with anything that departs from a majority Zionist Israeli Jewish point of view,” he told Al Jazeera.

But the proceedings against students were structured to prevent Palestinians from sharing their perspective or defence.

“Even where defence linguists were brought forward, their opinions were routinely dismissed or disregarded,” Mansour said. “Students’ identity was put on trial so explicitly that one committee even noted a student’s identification with children in Gaza could be ‘interpreted as offensive’, and questioned that student on why they didn’t identify with Israeli children.”

Historically, Article 17 of Israel’s Students’ Rights Law limited disciplinary powers against students to conduct connected to academic studies. But institutions expanded their jurisdiction over students’ lives after the war on Gaza began. They employed catch-all provisions like “unfitting conduct” and “harm to public peace”, as well as replacing legal thresholds with tests evaluating “public sensibilities”.

“These ‘public sensibilities’ and this ‘reasonable person’ were effectively interpreted by committees and tribunals to mean the Jewish Israeli public and the sentiment of the majority,” Mansour told Al Jazeera.

“By effectively turning emotions into legal authority, used to determine the legality of speech and its meaning, institutions created uncertainty around what type of speech is prohibited.”

According to Mansour, this approach resulted in a state of conditional inclusion for Palestinian students in Israeli universities .

“[Palestinians] remain students only for as long as their expression stays within boundaries set by the comfort of the majority, and the alignment with the broader Jewish-Israeli discourse,” he said.

Meanwhile, the Adalah report documented that Israeli academic institutions ignored widespread calls by Jewish-Israeli students for the annihilation and genocide of the Palestinian people in Gaza.

Commenting to the Times Higher Education on Wednesday, the Technion said the report was “part of a broader attempt to discredit Israeli academia and institutions”, and called the accusations “baseless”.

To justify these severe measures, institutions such as the Hebrew University of Jerusalem invoked the 1965 Yardor ruling, a “militant democracy” doctrine originally used during periods of military rule to suspend the protections of the law against perceived internal enemies.

Mansour explained that this legal manoeuvring is part of a broader, deeply entrenched system weighed against Palestinians in Israeli academia.

“We see this less as a testing ground for future expansion than as one expression of an existing system, one that has long treated Palestinian citizens as the ‘other’, a fifth column, an internal enemy, particularly when they express their Palestinian identity, national narrative, or engage in discourse considered illegitimate from a majority Zionist-Jewish-Israeli point of view,” Mansour said.

“[Academia is] one visible, well-evidenced part of a system that already spans multiple sectors in parallel,” he said. “One that continuously defines aspects of language, religion, culture and political symbols such as the Palestinian flag as markers of the enemy”.

Mansour called upon international human rights bodies to hold Israeli universities accountable for breaches of international law.

“We do believe that academic freedom, adherence to international law, and freedom of expression should be an absolute precondition for any academic partnership or collaboration,” Mansour told Al Jazeera.

“Our report clearly finds a structural, institutionalised repression, applied at scale across roughly 40 institutions. These are not isolated incidents – it’s a policy, which we call on these institutions to immediately end”.

That “institutionalised repression” has fundamentally altered the shared academic space in Israel, Mansour said.

“From our direct work with around 100 students, we can say that the impact has been substantial, and it has produced a chilling effect,” he concluded.

“The stakes were not limited to disciplinary proceedings: students were arrested, and in some cases held in detention in harsh conditions. Universities even reported their own students to the police”.

articles.title: Authorities identify 5 victims killed when Amazon-branded cargo plane overran runway in Miami
articles.summary: An airline cleaning company was mourning the loss of five employees who were identified as those killed Sunday when an Amazon-branded cargo plane overran the runway at Miami International Airport, striking the company’s van and a passenger SUV.
articles.body: An airline cleaning company was mourning the loss of five employees who were identified as those killed Sunday when an Amazon-branded cargo plane overran the runway at Miami International Airport, striking the company’s van and a passenger SUV. The deceased victims were Rolando Aleman, 55, Yoel Rodriguez Naranjo, 53, Julio C Pineda, 75, Carlos Acosta Fajardo, 53, and Javierkys Reyes Quevedo, 47, the Miami-Dade Sheriff’s Office said at a news conference Tuesday. They were all in the van, owned by Professional Ocean Service Corp., a contract cleaning company for airline companies. Five other people were injured in the crash and taken to the hospital, officials said. Eugenio Corredor, 79, and Ridoel Averhoff Diaz, 32, remain in critical condition, and Roosevelt Sebastian Perdomo Torres, 36, is stable. The two pilots of the Boeing 767-300 aircraft, Jaime Felipe Silva Molina, 37, and Joseph Carol, 55, were treated and released. The cleaning company said in a statement Tuesday that it was “heartbroken” by the deaths. “Our employees are far more than the people who work beside us each day, they are family, and they are deeply loved,” the statement read. “Our hearts and prayers are with every employee and every family whose lives have been forever changed. We grieve with those who lost a loved one and pray for the healing and recovery of those who were injured.” The Miami-Dade Sheriff’s Office said that the National Transportation Safety Board is leading the investigation into the crash. The aircraft was on its third trip that day when it overran the runway during a landing, NTSB Chair Jennifer Homendy said at a news conference Monday. Earlier Sunday, the plane traveled from Cincinnati to Miami, and then Miami to San Juan, Puerto Rico. It was returning from San Juan when it crashed. Homendy said that upon landing back in Miami, the plane overran the runway and struck navigational aids and equipment before hitting the cleaning company’s Ford van, which was transporting the crew inside the airport. The plane then careened through a perimeter fence and struck a Toyota SUV that was traveling on Northwest 67th Avenue outside the airport. The aircraft continued into the grass where it hit a fence line, which separated an area where Tesla robotaxis were stationed, Homendy said. She described the scene as “devastating” and said the van had been “torn apart.” Cellphone footage obtained by NBC South Florida showed someone jumping out of the plane after the crash. A photo sent to NBC News showed a crew member being taken away on a gurney at the airport. An Amazon spokesperson had previously said that the flight was operated by 21 Air. Keith Winters, 21 Air’s CEO, said in a message on its website that it is cooperating with federal investigators and offered condolences to the victims’ families. Homendy said it was too early to release much information about the factors that contributed to the crash, but said the plane’s flight data and cockpit voice recorder have been recovered.

articles.title: British widow faces deportation from Sweden after 22 years
articles.summary: A 78-year-old British woman is facing deportation for failing to fill out a Brexit residence application on time.
articles.body:
A 78-year-old British widow has told the BBC she is struggling to eat or sleep as the Swedish government threatens to deport her over a late post-Brexit residence application.

Joyce Thomas, a retired nurse, moved to Sweden 22 years ago with her husband, who passed away from cancer three years ago.

This came after they were informed by the Swedish authorities that they should have made a formal application to stay in the country after Brexit.

Thomas has since had numerous applications and appeals rejected, and Tuesday marks the latest deadline for her to leave voluntarily.

"This is absolute hell," she said from her home in Sweden.

"I can't sleep, I can't eat. You get up in the morning, you don't know what's going to happen."

The Swedish migration minister told the BBC that the government will "examine whether there are measures we can take to make the process easier for those affected" by some consequences of the EU-UK withdrawal agreement.

When the UK left the EU on 31 January 2020, British citizens stopped being EU citizens, which meant they could no longer stay in Sweden with right of residence status.

During a transitional period, British citizens could apply for residence status under the withdrawal agreement between the UK and the EU - which ended on 31 December 2021.

Thomas said she and her husband were unaware that they needed to submit an application and she was only informed of the rule once she attempted to re-enter the country in 2023.

After years of appeals, the Migrationsverket, the Swedish government agency responsible for migration, told her last month that her voluntary departure deadline was 8 September.

Her lawyers are arguing against the deportation, but she is still waiting to hear from the government.

Thomas said the possibility of having to leave her son, grandchildren, friends and husband's grave has become too much to bear.

"I'm tired, I really am tired and I'm not young anymore," she said.

"Where is the empathy? I've lived here for more than 20 years - I've got friends, I've got family."

According to Eurostat data, between 2021 and 2025, 2,490 UK nationals were ordered to leave Sweden. This is almost a third of more than 7,500 UK nationals ordered to leave the 27 EU Member States over this time period.

The Migrationsverket said it could not comment on Thomas's case without her consent and did not respond to a question about how many British nationals are at risk of deportation.

However, it told the Guardian last week that 458 British citizens had been deported or forcibly removed since Brexit.

Last month, a family told the BBC how their father, who has dementia and vascular parkinsonism and is living in full-time care in Sweden, was also threatened with removal after more than two decades in the country.

Swedish minister for migration, Johan Forssell, told the BBC that the current framework was implemented by a previous government and that it "will therefore look closely at the situation and examine whether there are measures we can take to make the process easier for those affected".

He did not address Thomas's case directly but said "the government believes the rules should be applied generously".

"The UK is a very important partner for Sweden, and we want British citizens who live and work in Sweden to be able to remain here," he said.

"We are currently in dialogue with the relevant Swedish authorities to get a clearer picture of what measures may be possible," he added.

A spokesperson from the the UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office said: "We welcome the statement from the Swedish authorities that they will look at this issue. We are ready to support them in doing so."
